newsitem.title: UK: IRA needs new assurances for truce - Morrison.
newsitem.headline: IRA needs new assurances for truce - Morrison.

text.p: Britain may have to give Irish republicans private guarantees it would not stall their entry to peace talks to pave the way for a new IRA truce, a former U.S. congressman said on Sunday.

Bruce Morrison, who is leading an independent fact-finding group in high-level talks on Northern Ireland, ruled out an early resumption of a 17-month Irish Republican Army ceasefire that collapsed in February.
"Folks ought not to be expecting it immediately around the corner from everything we've been told," he told Irish radio after a week of speculation about an early truce.

Morrison, who helped broker the original IRA ceasefire, had talks with Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm on Saturday. His five-day itinerary includes meetings with most key pro-British and pro-Irish parties.

He will meet British Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew on Monday and Irish Prime Minister John Bruton in Dublin on Tuesday and will brief White House officials and other American politicians when he returns to Washington.

The IRA resumed its war on British rule in Northern Ireland in February. It accused London of reneging on a deal to give Sinn Fein a seat in the peace talks by introducing a demand for the IRA to surrender its weapons.
Wrangling over "arms decommissioning" has blighted multi-party talks that started in June. Britain and Ireland have barred Sinn Fein while the IRA remains on a war footing.
Sinn Fein said they should be scrapped and replaced with a talks process that guarantees an end to what it dubs "British stalling" and gives the party an unconditional seat immediately.

"I would expect that it would not be likely there would be a new ceasefire if people believed that there was then going to be a new round of discussion about what else was required for Sinn Fein to become a meaningful part of the political negotations...," Morrison said.

"I could imagine to that extent the British would be expected to give assurances, not necessarily publicly, about the position they would take if the ceasefire were restored and what that would mean in terms of the political process moving forward."
Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief strategist, said on Saturday the peace process had died and a new one was needed.

He said it must be based on "inclusive negotiations" in a defined time frame, an end to the demand for early disarmament, and implementation of "confidence buidling measures", such as prisoner releases by Britain.

"This is the minimum I believe that Sinn Fein (would need) to go to the IRA to request a second ceasefire. I think that anything less than that is doomed to failure. That is a reality that must be faced," he told BBC radio.

Multi-party talks, chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, are due to resume on Monday. Hardline Protestant politicians say London and Dublin are using them as a cover to dilute the demand for a ceasefire and to give Sinn Fein a seat.

Britain and Ireland, hoping the IRA will call off its violence, have given assurances that the current talks are on a broad agenda in which republicans could press their case for a United Ireland republic.
Sinn Fein has spurned the assurances, saying pro-British politicians want to turn them into a single-item arms decommissioning conference.
